claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys is governed by grain-boundary density and distribution.
Grain-boundary density and distribution affect formation of a stable passivating surface oxide.
The proposed initial material is coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi HEA.
Hot rolling followed by annealing will introduce a refined grain structure in CoCrFeMnNi.
The refined grain structure acts as a barrier to dislocation movement.
The refined grain structure acts as a barrier to corrosion pathways.
Grain refinement enhances formation of a stable passivating surface oxide.
The stable passivating oxide improves resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Under saline exposure and cyclic loading, the processed alloy will have a 25% lower wear rate than the coarse-grained baseline.
Under saline exposure and cyclic loading, the processed alloy will have a 20% lower corrosion rate than the coarse-grained baseline.
Under saline exposure and cyclic loading, the processed alloy will have 35% lower combined wear-plus-corrosion degradation than the coarse-grained baseline.
The prediction should hold for high-entropy alloys having refined grain structures.
The prediction may fail for other material systems or operating conditions.
The stability of the refined grain structure under the proposed corrosive-mechanical environment is uncertain.
Failure of the processed alloy to improve both wear and corrosion resistance relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
